problem: ObjectNav methods either use sample-inefficient RL policies for mid-term goal selection or scene-completion models that must predict exact positions of unseen objects, which is hard and ambiguous (e.g. where a chair sits around a table).
motivation: Objects have stable distance relations (chairs are usually near tables) even when exact poses are unpredictable. A supervised distance predictor over frontier cells can be trained offline and plugged into a classical navigation stack.
key_idea: Predict, from a bird's-eye semantic map, a discretized shortest-path distance-to-target map on the exploration frontier, then pick mid-term goals from it with simple hand-designed strategies and FMM planning instead of RL.
insight: Predicting a coarse distance category is easier and more useful than exact scene completion or a continuous regression: discrete bins (SR 42.8 / SPL 23.1) beat continuous regression (41.2 / 20.4), and fine bins at short range matter more than long range (the [2,4,8,12] partition is worst). Distance-prediction accuracy is very low (avg precision 0.254), yet navigation still improves because the predicted direction is right, i.e. only relative ordering across frontier cells is needed. The dominant failure source is semantic mapping: TV is about 0% with the detector, while GT semantics give large gains.
method: Semantic mapping: SemExp-style BEV map with 15 semantic channels plus obstacle and explored channels, 5cm cells, built from Mask-RCNN on RGB-D plus pose.

Target distance prediction: a fully convolutional U-Net with 3 down and 3 up ResBlocks and skip connections. It takes a k×240×240 local semantic map and outputs n_b×n_T channels, i.e. 5 distance-range classes for each of the 6 target categories. Trained with pixel-wise cross-entropy near the frontier (class weights 5 to 1) on GT distance maps from random exploration, 1.2M samples.

Path-planning strategy (PP): choose the frontier cell minimizing path distance from the agent plus predicted distance (Eq. 1); if the target is seen, go to it; if all predictions are infinite, explore randomly.
Closest-First strategy (CF): choose the frontier cell with the smallest predicted distance (Eq. 2).
Door-Exploring-First strategy (DEF): a ResNet50 door/passage classifier restricts the goal to the frontier within a 120° sector when a door is detected (p≥0.5), otherwise CF.
Local planner: FMM on the obstacle channel gives the path and action. Baselines are RandomExp, FrontierExp, SemExp and SSCExp.

setting.backbone: Mask-RCNN (COCO pretrained) + ResNet-style U-Net distance predictor (trained from scratch) + ResNet50 door classifier + FMM planner
setting.training_data: 1.2M local semantic-map/GT distance-map samples from random exploration in 54 MP3D training scenes; the door classifier is trained separately
setting.action_space: mid-term goal on the local map, then FMM path planning to discrete low-level actions
setting.privileged: none for the main method (the '-GT' variants use GT local semantic maps; the GT distance map is used only for training)

results: On its own 1200-episode MP3D protocol, Ours-DEF reaches 43.6% SR / 0.232 SPL versus SemExp 41.0% / 0.197 (+2.6% SR, about +3.5% SPL) while using about 12% of the training samples (1.2M vs 10M). With GT semantics Ours-GT has SPL 0.566 versus SemExp-GT 0.522. In the real world the robot gets 84.7% SR over 150 episodes.
limitations: Depends heavily on semantic mapping quality: TV is about 0% in simulation, and detection or projection errors cause most failures.
Distance prediction accuracy is low (avg precision 0.254), and predictions are uncertain when related objects have not been fully explored.

Evaluated on a self-made 1200-episode protocol with 6 categories, not the standard challenge; the SSCExp baseline is a reimplementation with mismatched settings. The PP strategy gives zigzag paths and low SPL.
